analysis.one_liner: Extends tax breaks for investing capital gains in designated low-income and rural areas through 2033.
analysis.headline: Introduced June 3, 2025 with no cosponsors; the bill sits in the House Ways and Means Committee with no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: Opportunity zones are a tax program, created in 2017, that lets people who sell stocks or businesses defer and eventually reduce the tax on their capital gains if they reinvest that money in designated low-income census tracts. This bill would start a new round of zones from 2027 through 2033, tighten which tracts qualify, reserve a share of zones for rural areas, and enlarge the tax benefit: investors who hold for five years would get an extra 10% reduction in taxable gain, 30% in rural zones, and the bill specifically boosts a tax break for improving existing rural buildings, including data centers. It also adds detailed reporting rules for the investment funds and requires the Treasury Department to publish annual data on jobs, housing, and poverty in the zones.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors with unrealized capital gains — largely higher-income households and funds — who could park gains in the new zones and pay less tax. Developers building or rehabbing property in designated tracts, especially rural ones, get a larger basis step-up, and rural data center projects are singled out for a 50% adjustment. Residents of designated tracts may benefit if investment actually creates jobs and housing, which the bill's own new reporting rules are designed to test.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new round of qualified opportunity zone designations, chosen by governors, running January 1, 2027 through December 31, 2033.

Requires that at least 33% of new designations (or the greater of that and the national rural population share) go to entirely rural areas, and gives rural-zone investors a 30% basis increase instead of 10%.
Lets taxpayers elect to roll up to $10,000 of ordinary income (not just capital gains) into an opportunity fund.
Adds a 50% basis adjustment for improving existing structures in rural zones, a provision the bill text explicitly extends to data centers.

Tightens eligibility: tracts with median family income at or above 125% of the state or metro median are disqualified, and the income threshold for eligibility drops from 80% to 70% of area median, aiming designations at poorer places.

Requires opportunity funds to file detailed annual returns (assets, locations, NAICS codes, jobs, housing units) with penalties up to $250,000 for large funds that intentionally disregard the rules, and requires Treasury to publish annual public reports on where the money went, plus comparative studies of jobs, poverty, rents, and homeownership in designated versus similar non-designated tracts.

analysis.who_pays: The Treasury — that is, taxpayers generally — bears the cost of deferring and reducing tax on capital gains, a benefit available mainly to people who already have substantial investments. The existing program's original designations end December 31, 2026 under current law; this bill extends the incentive for seven more years.

drawbacks.text: The core benefit flows to people who already hold capital gains: an investor must have appreciated assets to defer, and the 10% basis increase plus the ordinary-income roll-in widen the tax advantage for those investors, with the revenue cost borne by the Treasury.

The bill's own reporting section acknowledges that outcomes are unproven: it directs Treasury to compare designated tracts against similar undesignated ones on unemployment, poverty, median income, rents, home ownership, and affordable housing — metrics that prior rounds of the program were never systematically tracked against.

The data center provision creates a targeted tax advantage for improving rural buildings for data center use, which may drive real estate investment without guaranteeing local jobs or lower costs for residents.

Extension of the incentive is automatic for any nominated tract that qualifies; the bill guarantees the tax benefit to investors for seven years while making community benefits a matter of later measurement rather than a condition of the tax break.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs a bigger, longer tax incentive for investors with genuinely useful transparency: mandatory fund reporting with real penalties and public Treasury data on jobs and housing. That accountability matters, because the benefit to residents of designated zones is indirect and uncertain, while the tax benefit to investors with capital gains is direct and certain. On balance, the certain gains flow to concentrated wealth and the uncertain gains to communities.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and has sat there since, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Kelly (R-PA) introduced H.R. 3687 on June 3, 2025, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
No further action has been taken since the referral to committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one yet; the bill has not moved, and current opportunity zone rules — set to run through the end of 2026 — remain in place.

for.name: Rep. Mike Kelly
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to renew and enhance opportunity zones and referred it to Ways and Means.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have been held and the bill has no cosponsors, so the partisan shape is not yet visible; the sponsor is a Republican on the majority side of the House.

industries.industry: Real estate developers and capital-gains investors
industries.note: The bill locks in the opportunity zone structure — public tax benefits routed through private investment funds — through 2033 and enlarges the benefit (10% basis increase, 30% in rural zones, a $10,000 ordinary-income roll-in). The investor gain is a certain tax reduction funded by forgone Treasury revenue; any community benefit is indirect and, per the bill's own reporting provisions, unmeasured until after the fact.

industries.industry: Data centers and rural commercial development
industries.note: A special rule gives a 50% basis adjustment for improving existing structures in rural zones, explicitly including data centers, making rural data center projects more tax-advantaged. New facilities can bring construction work and some jobs, but the benefit accrues first to the facility owners.

industries.industry: Rural small businesses and property owners
industries.note: Rural zones get priority designations and tripled basis step-ups, so qualifying rural businesses and property could attract investment that has historically gone to big-city zones. Whether that translates into local wages depends on what gets built.

analysis.trajectory: A standalone tax bill with zero cosponsors rarely reaches the House floor on its own; it will likely sit in Ways and Means unless opportunity zone renewal is folded into a broader tax package, which is the more common path for provisions like these.
